Stage 1 · Warm-up

Where do you end up?

Follow the route in your head. You do not have to say anything yet.

Start at the bus station. Follow the four instructions. Where are you?

1  Come out of the bus station and turn right.
2  Go straight on until you reach the roundabout.
3  Go past the supermarket and take the second turning on the left.
4  Cross the road. It’s the building opposite the pharmacy.

Read instruction 4 again if you are not sure.

Write it down

How do you get from your home to the nearest shop? Write three short instructions.

Talk about it
  • When did you last ask a stranger for directions? Did you understand the answer?
  • Do you use a map on your phone, or do you ask people?
Now speak — ask and answer these questions with a partner.
Answer these two out loud before you go on.

1  How do you usually find a place you have never been to?

2  When did you last get lost? What happened?

Then tell the class the one most surprising thing about your partner.

Stage 3 · Grammar

How the exchange works

No new tense today. Directions are imperatives, and the shape of the conversation matters as much as the words.

Read four lines from today’s recordings.
  • Please could you tell me how to get to the Jim Thompson House?
  • Go straight along this road — go past the shopping centre and keep going.
  • You’ll see the MBK shopping centre on the left.
  • So it’s left at the crossroads? Is that right?
What form are the instructions in?
The four moves
MoveWhat it doesLanguage
1 · AskStop someone politely and askExcuse me, could you tell me the way to…? · …how to get to…? · Is this the right way to…?
2 · GiveImperative + preposition of movementGo straight on · Turn left / right · Go past the bank · Cross the road · Take the second turning · Keep going until you reach…
3 · LocateSay where the place isIt’s on the left / right · on the corner · opposite the bank · next to the café
4 · Check & reassureThe listener repeats; the speaker confirmsSo it’s left at the crossroads? Is that right? — Yes, that’s right. · You can’t miss it. · Is it far? — About ten minutes.
Landmarks recycledthe street where the old cinema is · the building which has flags outside · the man who sells souvenirs
Prepositions of movement
  • along this road · past the bank · through the park
  • across the square · up / down the street
  • out of the station · into Station Road
  • until you reach… is what stops the instruction
What makes directions clear
  • One instruction at a time. Do not join three with and.
  • Give a landmark after each turn, not just the turn.
  • Say how far: about 200 metres, about ten minutes.
  • Let the other person repeat it back. That is where mistakes are caught.

IMPERATIVES. Just the bare verb: Go, Turn, Cross, Take, Keep going. No you, no tense.

PREPOSITIONS DO THE WORK. along, past, through, across, out of, into carry the movement.

THE EXCHANGE. Ask → give → locate → check back. The checking is not optional.

Not “You go past to the bank”, not “Cross through the road”, not “Take second turning” without the.

This is the last lesson of Unit 2. The Unit Test follows.

IMPERATIVES. An instruction in English is the bare verb with no subject: Go straight on. Turn left. Cross the road. Take the second turning. There is no tense to choose and no -s to add, which is why directions are one of the easiest things to say well — and why getting the preposition right matters so much.

PREPOSITIONS OF MOVEMENT. These carry the meaning. along a road (following its length), past a building (moving by it), through a park or a room (in one side and out the other), across a square or a road (side to side), out of a station, into a street, up or down a hill. Note that cross already contains ‘across’, so you say cross the road, never cross across or cross through.

SAYING WHEN TO STOP. An instruction without an end point is useless. English uses until: Keep going until you reach a crossroads. You can also give a distance (for about 200 metres) or a landmark (You’ll see the hospital on the left).

LOCATING THE PLACE. Once they are close, you place the building: on the left, on the right, on the corner, opposite the bank, next to the café, straight ahead. This is where the relative clauses from Lesson 5 come back: it’s the street where the old cinema is, the building which has flags outside.

THE SHAPE OF THE EXCHANGE. Listen to the three recordings and you will hear the same four moves every time: the stranger asks, the local gives the route, the local locates the building, and then — every time — the stranger repeats the route back and the local confirms. So it’s left at the crossroads? Is that right? — Yes, that’s right. Learners skip this step, and it is the step that catches mistakes.

The four to watch: “Go past to the bank” · “Cross through the road” · “Take second turning” (needs the) · “You go straight on” when an imperative is wanted.

Relative clauses from Lesson 5 describe the landmarks, and the Present Continuous from Lesson 4 tells the other person where you are right now. Unit 2 ends here.

Five phrases from the coursebook recordings. Navigate B1 · Audio 2.10 and 2.11

Full grammar reference — Directions: imperatives and prepositions of movement

Form

ImperativeGo straight on. · Turn left. · Cross the road.
Negative imperativeDon’t turn right at the lights.
Movementalong · past · through · across · over · into · out of · up · down · towards
Positionon the left / right · on the corner · opposite · next to · between
AskingCould you tell me the way to…? · Is this the right way to…?

When and why we use it

  • An imperative uses the plain verb with no subject and no to.
  • Give one instruction at a time, and add a landmark after every turn.
  • Until says when to stop: Keep going until you reach the roundabout.
  • Reassure at the end: You can’t miss it.

Signal words

first · then · after that · when you get to… · keep going until…

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Go to straight on. → Go straight on.No to before an adverb.
  • Turn on the left. → Turn left. / It’s on the left.Turn left, but on the left for position.
  • Cross through the road. → Cross the road.Cross already means ‘go across’.
  • Go past of the bank. → Go past the bank.No of after past.

Don’t confuse it with

Go past = along and beyond something. Cross = from one side to the other. Go through = in one side and out of the other.

Model 2 · City Library — How to find us

From the bus station — ten minutes on foot. Come out of the main entrance and turn right. Go straight on for about 200 metres until you reach the roundabout. Go past the supermarket and take the second turning on the left. The library is the grey building on the corner, opposite the pharmacy.

By car. Leave the main road at the roundabout and follow the signs to the city centre. There are twelve parking spaces behind the building.

Please note. The main entrance is closed on Sundays. On Sundays, please use the side door on Park Street.

If you cannot find us, telephone reception on 55 40 12 and a member of staff will meet you at the door.

Source note. Written for this course. It follows the shape that public libraries and museums use on their own ‘How to find us’ pages: a heading for each way of arriving, a walking time, a landmark after every turn, and a line telling you what to do if you cannot find the building.

Same route, two registers
  • One instruction per message in Model 1 — the reader is walking. One heading per way of arriving in Model 2 — the reader is planning.
  • Short forms and an emoji in Model 1: I’m, can’t, See you in 5. Full forms and no emoji in Model 2: cannot, please, a member of staff.
  • Model 1 can ask Now what? Model 2 cannot answer, so it ends with what to do if you get lost.
  • Both do the same four things: start point → instructions with a landmark after every turn → the door → reassurance.
  • A distance in both: about 200 metres, ten minutes on foot.
Your plan — use it in Stage 7
  • 1 Start point. Where does the reader begin? From the bus station… / I’m at the bus stop now.
  • 2 The route. One instruction at a time, and a landmark after every turn. Put one distance or one time in.
  • 3 The door. on the left · on the corner · opposite the… · the street where…
  • 4 The ending. To a friend: You can’t miss it. To the public: If you cannot find us, please…
Stage 7 · Now you

Ask, give, check

Both roles. The checking back is half the task.

Useful language

Excuse me, could you tell me the way to…?  Is this the right way to…?

Go straight on · Turn left/right · Go past… · Cross… · Take the second turning · Keep going until…

It’s on the left · on the corner · opposite…  So it’s…? Is that right?  You can’t miss it.

Writing for the public: From the bus station — ten minutes on foot · Follow the signs to… · Please use… · If you cannot find us, telephone…

Work in pairs. One asks, one gives. Then swap.
Choose a card and write the message thread.
Card A

Your partner is at the nearest bus stop and is coming to your home. Talk them all the way to your front door.

Card B

Your partner is a tourist in your town, standing in the main square. Direct them to the railway station.

Round 1. A asks and must repeat the route back at least once. B gives the directions with a landmark after every turn.

Round 2. Swap cards and roles. B now asks.

Write it

Use the four-move plan from Stage 6 and choose one:

A — to a friend. Write a thread of six to eight messages. One instruction per message, a landmark after every turn, one distance, and end with You can’t miss it.

B — for the public. Write a short How to find us note for your school, your office or your home. A heading for each way of arriving, a walking time, a landmark after every turn, and a last line telling the reader what to do if they cannot find the door. Full forms, no emoji.

Check six things: bare imperatives, the right prepositions, a landmark after each turn, one until or a distance, a closing line, and one register all the way through — short forms in A, full forms in B.
